% Section 1: Introduction (compressed, 669→~550 words)

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Large language models are increasingly deployed for zero-shot information extraction~\cite{li2023codeie,sainz2024gollie,wei2023zeroshot}, but when generating relation triples $(h, r, t)$, neither entity is guaranteed to carry a type consistent with the ontology's domain/range constraints for $r$.
We call such outputs \emph{domain/range violations}---structurally valid triples that are ontologically invalid.
In a systematic study, we find violations are pervasive: 15.4\% of triples on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} and 18.7\% on DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred}, driven by \emph{constraint tightness} (few valid type pairs per relation) rather than ontology scale.
Relations with tight constraints exhibit far higher rates (\textsc{Compare}: 42.4\%) than loosely constrained ones (\textsc{Used-for}: 0.8\%).

Existing approaches leave a fundamental gap.
Schema-informed prompting reduces violations by 62\% on average but is per-relation unreliable---violations for \textsc{Evaluate-for} actually \emph{increase} by 5.8\,pp.
Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{dong2025xgrammar,willard2023outlines,beurer-kellner2023lmql} guarantees syntactic well-formedness but cannot encode cross-field semantic constraints.
Post-hoc validation wastes compute on discarded outputs and cannot redirect probability mass during decoding.
Training-based approaches~\cite{sainz2024gollie,lu2022uie} provide only soft guidance that cannot eliminate violations.

We propose \textbf{OntoCoDec} (\textbf{Onto}logy-\textbf{Co}mpiled \textbf{Dec}oding), a framework that compiles an IE ontology into two composable layers of decoding-time constraints.
The \emph{grammar layer} enforces JSON well-formedness and vocabulary validity via XGrammar.
The \emph{semantic layer} maintains a stateful entity registry during generation: as entities are decoded, the registry records type assignments; when relation arguments are generated, dynamic logit masking restricts output to types compatible with the relation's domain/range specification.
The layers compose via bitwise AND with an \emph{enabling dependency}: the grammar layer guarantees vocabulary membership, enabling the semantic layer to look up domain/range rules.
On SciERC, OntoCoDec reduces DR violations from 15.37\% to 0.93\% ($\downarrow$94\%) while remaining F1-neutral ($+$0.13\,pp).

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item The first systematic study of ontological constraint violations in LLM-based IE, showing that violation rates are driven by constraint tightness rather than ontology size, and that prompt-level intervention is per-relation unreliable.
    \item OntoCoDec, a two-layer compiled constraint framework that enforces cross-field type validity during autoregressive IE---the first to extend grammar-constrained decoding with semantic ontology constraints.
    \item Empirical validation on 2 models $\times$ 2 datasets: DR $\downarrow$94\% on SciERC and $\downarrow$45--90\% on DocRED at zero F1 cost, with model-agnostic generalization.
\end{enumerate}

5	\section{Method}
6	\label{sec:method}
7	
8	We present OntoCoDec, a two-layer constrained decoding framework that compiles ontology schemas into token-level masks enforced during autoregressive generation.
9	The grammar layer (\S\ref{sec:grammar}) guarantees structural validity—well-formed JSON with ontology-vocabulary membership—while the semantic layer (\S\ref{sec:semantic}) enforces domain/range type constraints via a stateful entity registry.
10	We describe the problem formulation (\S\ref{sec:formulation}), each layer, and two decoding strategies (\S\ref{sec:strategies}).
11	Formal analysis of constraint composition is deferred to Section~\ref{sec:composition}.
12	
13	
14	\subsection{Problem Formulation}
15	\label{sec:formulation}
16	
17	\paragraph{IE as structured generation.}
18	Given an input text $x$, a language model generates a structured JSON output $y$:
19	%
20	\begin{equation}\label{eq:output-schema}
21	\resizebox{.88\columnwidth}{!}{$\displaystyle
22	  y = \bigl\{\texttt{entities}: [\{n_i, \tau_i\}],\; \texttt{relations}: [\{h_j, t_j, r_j, \tau^h_j, \tau^t_j\}]\bigr\}
23	$}
24	\end{equation}
25	%
26	where each entity has a name $n_i$ and type $\tau_i \in \mathcal{E}$, and each relation specifies head $h_j$, tail $t_j$, relation type $r_j \in \mathcal{R}$, and head/tail entity types $\tau^h_j, \tau^t_j$.
27	
28	\paragraph{Ontology schema.}
29	An ontology $\mathcal{O} = (\mathcal{E}, \mathcal{R}, \operatorname{dom}, \operatorname{range})$ defines entity types $\mathcal{E}$, relation types $\mathcal{R}$, and functions $\operatorname{dom}, \operatorname{range}: \mathcal{R} \to 2^{\mathcal{E}}$ specifying permitted head and tail types for each relation.
30	
31	\paragraph{Ontology compliance.}
32	A triple $(h, r, t)$ with $\operatorname{type}(h) = \tau^h$, $\operatorname{type}(t) = \tau^t$ is \emph{type-valid} w.r.t.\ $\mathcal{O}$ iff:
33	%
34	\begin{equation}\label{eq:type-valid}
35	  \tau^h \in \operatorname{dom}(r) \;\wedge\; \tau^t \in \operatorname{range}(r).
36	\end{equation}
37	%
38	Our goal is a decoding strategy maximizing $P(y \mid x)$ subject to ontology compliance: all triples must be type-valid under $\mathcal{O}$, and $y$ must be well-formed JSON conforming to Eq.~\eqref{eq:output-schema}.
39	
40	\paragraph{Constraint decidability.}
41	Not all ontology constraints are enforceable at every point during left-to-right generation.
42	We distinguish three classes by \emph{prefix-decidability}:
43	%
44	\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,nosep]
45	  \item \textbf{Local constraints} depend only on the current token position.
46	    Entity-type membership ($\tau_i \in \mathcal{E}$) and relation-vocabulary membership ($r_j \in \mathcal{R}$) are local.
47	  \item \textbf{Prefix-decidable constraints} depend on previously generated context.
48	    Domain/range constraints are prefix-decidable: once head type and relation type are generated, valid tail types are fully determined.
49	  \item \textbf{Non-local constraints} depend on information not yet generated (e.g., forward coreference) and fall outside single-pass decoding.
50	\end{enumerate}
51	%
52	The grammar layer handles class~(1); the semantic layer handles class~(2).
53	
54	
55	\subsection{Grammar Layer}
56	\label{sec:grammar}
57	
58	The grammar layer compiles $\mathcal{O}$ into a context-free grammar (CFG) enforced at every decoding step via logit masking.
59	This compilation proceeds in two stages.
60	
61	\paragraph{Schema-to-grammar compilation.}
62	We generate a JSON Schema encoding the structure in Eq.~\eqref{eq:output-schema} with \texttt{enum} constraints restricting entity types to $\mathcal{E}$ and relation types to $\mathcal{R}$.
63	This schema is compiled into an EBNF grammar via XGrammar~\cite{dong2025xgrammar}, producing a pushdown automaton tracking JSON structure and enum membership.
64	
65	\paragraph{Logit masking.}
66	At step $t$, the automaton computes grammar-valid tokens $G(t) \subseteq V$; all others receive logits $-\infty$.
67	This simultaneously enforces: (i)~structural validity (well-formed JSON), (ii)~relation vocabulary membership ($r_j \in \mathcal{R}$), and (iii)~entity type membership ($\tau_i \in \mathcal{E}$).
68	Domain/range constraints are \emph{not} enforced, as they depend on entity types within each triple—the gap filled by the semantic layer.
69	
70	\paragraph{Empirical profile.}
71	On SciERC, grammar constraints eliminate relation vocabulary violations entirely (1.39\%\,$\to$\,0\%) and entity type violations entirely (0.40\%\,$\to$\,0\%), with no measurable F1 impact.
72	Domain/range violations remain effectively unchanged (15.37\%\,$\to$\,14.84\%), confirming that grammar constraints enforce structural but not semantic validity.
73	
74	
75	\subsection{Semantic Layer}
76	\label{sec:semantic}
77	
78	The semantic layer enforces domain/range constraints through a stateful logits processor maintaining an entity registry during generation.
79	
80	\subsubsection{Entity Registry}
81	\label{sec:entity-registry}
82	
83	As the model generates the entity list, the semantic layer builds a registry $\mathcal{D}: \text{name} \to \text{type}$ mapping each entity to its declared type.
84	This registry is populated incrementally: when the model completes an entry $\{n_i, \tau_i\}$, the pair $(n_i, \tau_i)$ is added to $\mathcal{D}$.
85	The registry is then consulted during relation generation to look up the declared types of head and tail entities.
86	
87	\subsubsection{Position Detection}
88	\label{sec:position-detection}
89	
90	At each step $t$, the processor determines which field is currently being generated by pattern-matching on the decoded prefix.
91	We define five field positions---\textsc{EntityType}, \textsc{RelationType}, \textsc{HeadType}, \textsc{TailType}, and \textsc{FreeText}---identified via JSON key patterns (e.g., tokens following \texttt{"head\_type":} indicate \textsc{HeadType}).
92	Semantic masks activate only at type-bearing positions (\textsc{HeadType}, \textsc{TailType}).
93	
94	\subsubsection{Dynamic Masking}
95	\label{sec:dynamic-masking}
96	
97	At type-bearing positions, the processor computes a semantic mask $S(t) \subseteq V$ restricting generation to type-valid tokens.
98	
99	\paragraph{Head type masking.}
100	At a \textsc{HeadType} position, the processor considers the entity registry $\mathcal{D}$ and the current relation type $r_j$ (if already generated).
101	If $h_j \in \mathcal{D}$ and $\mathcal{D}[h_j] \in \operatorname{dom}(r_j)$, the mask allows only that registered type: $S(t) = \{\operatorname{tok}(\mathcal{D}[h_j])\}$, ensuring consistency with both the entity list and domain constraints.
102	Otherwise, if $r_j$ is known, the mask falls back to all domain-valid types: $S(t) = \{\operatorname{tok}(\tau) : \tau \in \operatorname{dom}(r_j)\}$.
103	If $r_j$ is unavailable, no semantic mask is applied.
104	
105	\paragraph{Tail type masking.}
106	At a \textsc{TailType} position, valid tail types are computed from $\operatorname{range}(r_j)$; if $t_j \in \mathcal{D}$, the mask further restricts to the registered type when range-valid.
107	This implements the core prefix-decidable constraint: once $(h_j, r_j, \tau^h_j)$ are known, valid $\tau^t_j$ values are fully determined by $\operatorname{range}(r_j)$.
108	
109	\paragraph{Implementation.}
110	Each $\tau \in \mathcal{E}$ is mapped to the token ID of its first subword token; we pre-verify uniqueness across all entity types, which holds for both SciERC and DocRED (6 types each) with the Qwen3-8B tokenizer.
111	The semantic mask is applied by setting logits of disallowed first-token IDs to $-\infty$.
112	
113	\subsubsection{Grammar-Semantic Interaction}
114	\label{sec:interaction}
115	
116	The final mask is the conjunction of $G(t)$ and $S(t)$, permitting only tokens satisfying both layers (formalized in \S\ref{sec:composition}).
117	This embodies an \emph{enabling dependency}: semantic lookup requires relation types to be valid members of $\mathcal{R}$, guaranteed only by the grammar layer.
118	Without grammar enforcement, the model may generate out-of-vocabulary relation types for which no $\operatorname{dom}$/$\operatorname{range}$ rules exist.
119	Empirically, semantic-only constraints reduce DR by only 24\% (15.37\%\,$\to$\,11.65\%) while failing to eliminate vocabulary violations; the full combination achieves 94\% DR reduction.
120	When $S(t) \cap G(t) = \emptyset$---the semantic layer would mask out all grammar-valid tokens---the system falls back to grammar-only control, preserving structural validity at the cost of a potential type violation.
121	This \emph{grammar-first invariant} reflects a deliberate priority ordering: structural integrity is a hard constraint, while type violations are soft errors detectable by downstream validation.
122	
123	
124	\subsection{Decoding Strategies}
125	\label{sec:strategies}
126	
127	\paragraph{S1: Single-pass decoding.}
128	Both constraint layers are active throughout a single generation pass.
129	The entity registry is populated as entities are generated and immediately available for relation-level type checking.
130	This is the simpler and recommended strategy, achieving strong constraint enforcement with higher relation F1 than the two-pass alternative.
131	
132	\paragraph{S2: Two-pass decoding.}\label{sec:s2}
133	The first pass generates only entities under grammar constraints; the extracted entities compile an input-dependent grammar that additionally constrains head and tail names to match declared entities.
134	The second pass generates relations under this tighter grammar plus semantic constraints.
135	Detailed comparison is provided in the appendix.
136

1	% Section: Constraint Composition (compressed, 787→~500 words)
2	
3	At each decoding step $t$, let $G(t) \subseteq V$ and $S(t) \subseteq V$ denote the tokens permitted by the grammar and semantic layers, respectively.
4	The final mask is their conjunction:
5	%
6	\begin{equation}\label{eq:composition}
7	  M_{\text{final}}(t) = M_{\text{grammar}}(t) \;\wedge\; M_{\text{semantic}}(t),
8	\end{equation}
9	%
10	so a token is allowed only if it satisfies \emph{both} structural and type-level constraints.
11	The conjunction is asymmetric: $S(t)$ is defined only over $G(t)$, reflecting the enabling dependency (\S\ref{sec:method})---the semantic layer requires the relation type to belong to $\mathcal{R}$, a property guaranteed only by the grammar layer.
12	
13	\paragraph{Grammar-First Fallback.}
14	When $S(t) \cap G(t) = \emptyset$---tight constraints leave no token that is both grammar-valid and semantically valid---na\"{\i}ve masking would force selection of a grammar-invalid token, breaking JSON structure.
15	We enforce a \emph{grammar-first fallback}: if no semantically valid token survives grammar filtering, semantic masking is skipped and the grammar layer alone controls selection.
16	Structural integrity is a hard constraint; a type violation is a soft error detectable by downstream validation.
17	
18	\paragraph{Constraint Tightness.}
19	We define the tightness of relation $r$ as:
20	%
21	\begin{equation}\label{eq:tightness}
22	  \tau(r) = 1 - \frac{|\mathcal{V}(r)|}{|\mathcal{T}|^2},
23	\end{equation}
24	%
25	where $\mathcal{V}(r)$ is the set of valid type pairs and $\mathcal{T}$ the entity type vocabulary.
26	The mean tightness $\bar{\tau} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|}\sum_{r} \tau(r)$ characterizes ontology restrictiveness.
27	Tighter constraints eliminate more grammar-valid tokens at type-bearing positions, increasing fallback frequency and residual DR.
28	This dual-factor mechanism---tightness $\times$ baseline model violation rate---explains the cross-dataset pattern: SciERC ($\bar{\tau}{=}0.333$, 24 valid pairs/relation) achieves 94--99\% DR reduction, while DocRED ($\bar{\tau}{=}0.842$, 5.68 pairs) achieves 45--90\%, with the residual modulated by model-specific baselines (\S\ref{sec:cross-model}).
29	
30	\paragraph{Decidability Taxonomy.}
31	We classify ontology constraints by when sufficient information becomes available:
32	%
33	\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,nosep]
34	  \item \textbf{Local}: require only the current token (entity/relation vocabulary membership). Handled by the grammar layer.
35	  \item \textbf{Prefix-decidable}: require the decoded prefix (domain/range constraints). Handled by the semantic layer via the entity registry.
36	  \item \textbf{Non-local}: require information not yet generated (forward coreference). Outside the scope of single-pass decoding; partially addressed by the two-pass strategy (S2, \S\ref{sec:s2}).
37	\end{enumerate}

%  (a) Core result

\paragraph{Core result: DR elimination at zero F1 cost.}
The full two-layer constraint configuration (S1) reduces domain/range
violations from 15.37\% to 0.93\%, a 94\% relative reduction,
% phase2_scierc_unconstrained: DR=0.1537; phase2_scierc_full_s1: DR=0.0093

% bootstrap: delta=+0.13pp, CI=[-0.24,+0.58], p=0.5824

that constraint enforcement is F1-neutral on this dataset.

\textsc{Compare}, from 33.54\% to 1.21\% on \textsc{Feature-of}, and
reach 0\% on four of seven relation types
(\textsc{Conjunction}, \textsc{Hyponym-of}, \textsc{Part-of},
\textsc{Used-for}).
% phase2_scierc_full_s1 per_relation_dr: Compare=0.0282,
%   Feature-of=0.0121, Hyponym-of=0, Part-of=0, Used-for=0, Conjunction=0
However, full constraint enforcement elevates cross-field consistency
violations from 0.08\% to 9.90\%;
% phase2_scierc_unconstrained: CF=0.0008; phase2_scierc_full_s1: CF=0.099
we analyze this trade-off in Section~\ref{sec:discussion}.

% ──────────────────────────────────────────

% ──────────────────────────────────────────

Grammar-only constraints completely eliminate both relation vocabulary
violations (1.39\%\,$\to$\,0\%) and entity type violations
(0.40\%\,$\to$\,0\%), with no measurable impact on F1
(R-F1 8.23, E-F1 30.98).
% phase2_scierc_grammar_only: RV=0, ET=0, R-F1=0.0823, E-F1=0.3098

(15.37\%\,$\to$\,14.84\%, $-$0.53\,pp), confirming that grammar
constraints enforce output structure---valid JSON, correct relation
vocabulary, valid entity types---but do not address cross-field
semantic constraints.
% phase2_scierc_grammar_only: DR=0.1484
The grammar layer thus provides two categories of violation elimination
at zero cost, establishing the structural preconditions on which the
semantic layer depends.

%  (c) Enabling dependency
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Enabling dependency: grammar enables semantic enforcement.}
Applying semantic constraints alone reduces DR by only 24\%
(15.37\%\,$\to$\,11.65\%) and, critically, cannot eliminate
relation vocabulary violations (RV\,=\,1.51\%) or entity type
violations (ET\,=\,0.40\%).
% phase2_scierc_semantic_only: DR=0.1165, RV=0.0151, ET=0.004

relative to the semantic-only configuration
(11.65\%\,$\to$\,0.93\%).
% phase2_scierc_full_s1: DR=0.0093; delta=(11.65-0.93)/11.65=0.920

additivity: without grammar-enforced vocabulary constraints, the
semantic layer encounters out-of-vocabulary relation types for which
no domain/range rules exist, rendering its type checking ineffective.
The two layers are therefore complementary with a prerequisite
structure---grammar must be active for semantic constraints to reach
their full enforcement capacity.

%  (d) S1 vs S2
% ──────────────────────────────────────────

% phase2_scierc_full_s1: DR=0.0093, R-F1=0.0836, triples=1729

configurations exhibit substantially elevated CF relative to the
unconstrained baseline (0.08\%), indicating that two-pass decoding
does not resolve the cross-field consistency trade-off
(Section~\ref{sec:discussion}).
% phase2_scierc_full_s2: CF=0.0803; phase2_scierc_full_s1: CF=0.099
The two-pass separation offers no clear advantage over single-pass

1	\section{Related Work}
2	\label{sec:related_work}
3	
4	\paragraph{Grammar-Constrained Decoding.}
5	XGrammar~\cite{dong2025xgrammar}, Outlines~\cite{willard2023outlines}, Guidance~\cite{guidance2023}, and LMQL~\cite{beurer-kellner2023lmql} have made grammar-constrained decoding the standard for structured LLM output, ensuring every token belongs to a grammar-valid continuation.
6	DOMINO~\cite{beurer-kellner2024domino} and ASAp~\cite{park2024grammar} further address distribution distortion, making grammar enforcement statistically principled.
7	However, these methods operate at the syntactic level---they ensure format validity but cannot enforce cross-field semantic constraints such as ontology domain/range rules.
8	
9	\paragraph{Semantic Constrained Decoding for Code.}
10	In code generation, constrained decoding has been extended to enforce semantic properties: Synchromesh~\cite{synchromesh_iclr2022} enforces type and scope constraints via dynamic token masks; PICARD~\cite{scholak2021picard} performs incremental SQL parsing to reject type-invalid tokens; MGD~\cite{mgd_neurips2023} applies static-analysis monitors for type checking at decode time; and \citet{pldi2025_type_constrained_codegen} compile full type systems into prefix automata for logits masking.
11	These demonstrate that richer-than-CFG constraints are feasible at decode time, but exclusively in the code domain---OntoCoDec migrates this paradigm to information extraction.
12	
13	\paragraph{Vocabulary and Type-Constrained Generation.}
14	\citet{roth_yih_2004} establish that relational type compatibility should be a hard constraint via integer linear programming, though applied post-hoc; see also~\cite{xie2016tkrl}.
15	GENRE~\cite{decao2021genre}, NeuroLogic~\cite{lu2021neurologic}, AdaKGC~\cite{adakgc_emnlp2023}, GCD~\cite{geng2023gcd}, and GoLLIE~\cite{sainz2024gollie} constrain \emph{which tokens} can appear (vocabulary membership) but not \emph{which type combinations} are valid for a given relation---OntoCoDec enforces relational constraints where the valid set depends on the relation type generated earlier in the same sequence.
16	
17	\paragraph{Structural Constraints via Training.}
18	TANL~\cite{paolini2021tanl}, REBEL~\cite{cabot2021rebel}, UIE~\cite{lu2022uie}, GoLLIE~\cite{sainz2024gollie}, KnowCoder~\cite{knowcoder_acl2024}, and CodeIE~\cite{li2023codeie} encode IE structure through training or schema-as-code prompting.
19	These provide \emph{soft} guidance---the model learns to prefer valid outputs but cannot guarantee compliance, as shown by non-trivial violation rates even in fine-tuned systems.
20	OntoCoDec provides complementary \emph{hard} enforcement that is training-free and composable with these methods.
21	
22	\paragraph{Post-hoc Ontology Validation.}
23	ODKE+~\cite{khorshidi2025odke} uses ontology snippets as prompt context; OntoGPT~\cite{spires_2024} validates outputs against ontologies in a second pass; OntoLogX~\cite{ontologx_2025} applies SHACL validation with iterative re-prompting, reducing violations by ${\sim}10\times$ across correction rounds.
24	These detect-then-fix approaches waste compute on violated outputs, whereas OntoCoDec \emph{prevents} violations during decoding by redirecting probability mass to valid alternatives.
25	
26	\paragraph{Quality Impact of Constrained Decoding.}
27	CRANE~\cite{banerjee2025crane} shows grammar restrictions suppress chain-of-thought reasoning, \citet{schall2025hiddencost} find 10--30\% degradation on reasoning tasks, and \citet{tam2024letmespeak} demonstrate that format constraints harm reasoning benchmarks.
28	However, \citet{tam2024letmespeak}'s results also show extraction-style tasks are robust to---or benefit from---constraints, and IE is fundamentally extraction rather than reasoning.
29	OntoCoDec confirms this: violations decrease by 94\% on SciERC with zero F1 degradation, as constraints target only type tokens while leaving entity spans unconstrained.
30	
31	\medskip
32	\noindent
33	OntoCoDec is the first system to automatically compile IE ontology domain/range constraints into token-level semantic masks, extending grammar-constrained decoding from syntactic to semantic enforcement for information extraction.
34

% Section: Constraint Composition (compressed, 787→~500 words)

At each decoding step $t$, let $G(t) \subseteq V$ and $S(t) \subseteq V$ denote the tokens permitted by the grammar and semantic layers, respectively.
The final mask is their conjunction:
%
\begin{equation}\label{eq:composition}
  M_{\text{final}}(t) = M_{\text{grammar}}(t) \;\wedge\; M_{\text{semantic}}(t),
\end{equation}
%
so a token is allowed only if it satisfies \emph{both} structural and type-level constraints.
The conjunction is asymmetric: $S(t)$ is defined only over $G(t)$, reflecting the enabling dependency (\S\ref{sec:method})---the semantic layer requires the relation type to belong to $\mathcal{R}$, a property guaranteed only by the grammar layer.

\paragraph{Grammar-First Fallback.}
When $S(t) \cap G(t) = \emptyset$---tight constraints leave no token that is both grammar-valid and semantically valid---na\"{\i}ve masking would force selection of a grammar-invalid token, breaking JSON structure.
We enforce a \emph{grammar-first fallback}: if no semantically valid token survives grammar filtering, semantic masking is skipped and the grammar layer alone controls selection.
Structural integrity is a hard constraint; a type violation is a soft error detectable by downstream validation.

\paragraph{Constraint Tightness.}
We define the tightness of relation $r$ as:
%
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tightness}
  \tau(r) = 1 - \frac{|\mathcal{V}(r)|}{|\mathcal{T}|^2},
\end{equation}
%
where $\mathcal{V}(r)$ is the set of valid type pairs and $\mathcal{T}$ the entity type vocabulary.
The mean tightness $\bar{\tau} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|}\sum_{r} \tau(r)$ characterizes ontology restrictiveness.
Tighter constraints eliminate more grammar-valid tokens at type-bearing positions, increasing fallback frequency and residual DR.
This dual-factor mechanism---tightness $\times$ baseline model violation rate---explains the cross-dataset pattern: SciERC ($\bar{\tau}{=}0.333$, 24 valid pairs/relation) achieves 94--99\% DR reduction, while DocRED ($\bar{\tau}{=}0.842$, 5.68 pairs) achieves 45--90\%, with the residual modulated by model-specific baselines (\S\ref{sec:cross-model}).

\paragraph{Decidability Taxonomy.}
We classify ontology constraints by when sufficient information becomes available:
%
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,nosep]
  \item \textbf{Local}: require only the current token (entity/relation vocabulary membership). Handled by the grammar layer.
  \item \textbf{Prefix-decidable}: require the decoded prefix (domain/range constraints). Handled by the semantic layer via the entity registry.
  \item \textbf{Non-local}: require information not yet generated (forward coreference). Outside the scope of single-pass decoding; partially addressed by the two-pass strategy (S2, \S\ref{sec:s2}).
\end{enumerate}

\paragraph{Setup.}
We evaluate Qwen3-8B~\cite{qwen2025qwen3} under zero-shot greedy decoding on two IE benchmarks:
\textbf{SciERC}~\cite{luan2018scierc} (551 test sentences, 7 relations, avg.\ 26.1 valid type pairs per relation) and \textbf{DocRED}~\cite{yao2019docred} (998 dev documents, 96 relations, avg.\ 5.68 valid pairs).
We measure four violation categories: \textbf{Domain/Range (DR)} violations where $(\mathrm{type}(h), \mathrm{type}(t)) \notin \sigma(r)$; \textbf{Relation Vocabulary (RV)} where $r \notin \mathcal{R}$; \textbf{Entity Type (ET)} where $e \notin \mathcal{E}$; and \textbf{Cross-Field Consistency (CF)} where the same entity receives different types across triples.
Cross-model validation with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct is reported in \S\ref{sec:cross-model}.

\paragraph{Violation distribution.}
Table~\ref{tab:prompt_comparison} reports violation rates.
DR violations affect 15.37\% of triples on SciERC and 18.70\% on DocRED---comparable rates despite a 14$\times$ difference in ontology size---indicating that violation severity is driven by \emph{constraint tightness} rather than ontology scale.
RV violations on DocRED are dramatically higher (28.90\% vs.\ 1.39\%), indicating that 96 relation types exceed the model's capacity to reproduce a target vocabulary from a single prompt.
Per-relation rates (Figure~\ref{fig:per_relation_dr}) vary by over 40 percentage points: \textsc{Compare} at 42.4\% vs.\ \textsc{Used-for} at 0.76\%, correlating with tightness---tight constraints (few valid type pairs) produce systematic failures.

GoLLIE~\cite{sainz2024gollie} expresses annotation guidelines as Python dataclass definitions and fine-tunes Code-LLaMA to generate typed code, achieving strong zero-shot transfer to unseen IE schemas by leveraging the implicit type structure of programming languages.
KnowCoder~\cite{knowcoder_acl2024} takes this further by encoding 29K entity types from Wikidata as a Python class hierarchy, training a Code-LLM to generate structured extraction code that implicitly respects type inheritance---the most comprehensive schema-as-code approach to date.
CodeIE~\cite{li2023codeie} similarly reformulates IE as code generation, leveraging the structural regularity of programming languages to reduce output format errors.
ADELIE~\cite{qi2024adelie} uses SFT and DPO to align LLMs on IE tasks, achieving state-of-the-art results among open-source models while preserving general capabilities, though compliance with ontological constraints remains a learned soft preference rather than a guarantee.
In the supervised setting, joint entity-relation architectures such as SpERT~\cite{eberts2020spert} and PFN~\cite{yan2021pfn} enforce type consistency implicitly through shared representations: SpERT classifies entity spans and relation pairs in a single BERT pass with span-level negative sampling, while PFN decomposes feature encoding into entity-specific, relation-specific, and shared partitions via gating mechanisms.
These models achieve strong performance but are limited to fixed, predefined schemas and cannot generalize to unseen ontologies without retraining---precisely the zero-shot, ontology-portable scenario that OntoCoDec targets.
EnriCo~\cite{zaratiana2024enrico} applies Answer Set Programming (ASP) constraints during decoding of joint entity-relation extraction models, enforcing structural type compatibility at generation time---a decoding-time approach, though with model-specific, manually authored constraints rather than ontology-driven compilation.
Training-based methods provide \emph{soft} structural guidance---the model learns to prefer valid outputs but cannot guarantee compliance at inference time, as demonstrated by non-trivial violation rates even in fine-tuned systems.
Importantly, training-based and decoding-time approaches are complementary rather than competing: a system like GoLLIE could be combined with OntoCoDec's constraint layers, using fine-tuning to maximize the probability of valid outputs while decoding-time enforcement eliminates residual violations.
OntoCoDec provides \emph{hard} decoding-time enforcement that is training-free, automatically compiled from ontology schemas, and composable with any of these training-based approaches.

% ===========================================================================
% Paradigm 4: Type-Checking / Ontology Validation
% ===========================================================================
\paragraph{Post-hoc Ontology Validation.}
Rather than constraining generation, several methods validate LLM outputs against ontological rules after generation, applying a detect-then-fix paradigm.
ODKE+~\cite{khorshidi2025odke} dynamically generates ontology snippets containing domain/range constraints as prompt context, achieving 98.8\% precision across 195 predicates at web scale---but constraint adherence relies on prompt-level guidance, not enforcement, leaving residual violations unaddressed.
SPIRES/OntoGPT~\cite{spires_2024} provides an ontology-based extraction framework that grounds LLM outputs against OBO ontologies post-generation, validating extracted entities and relations through ontology lookup and correcting mismatches in a second pass---representing the prompt-then-validate paradigm in the biomedical domain.
OntoLogX~\cite{ontologx_2025} applies SHACL validation to LLM-generated knowledge graphs, iteratively re-prompting the LLM to correct constraint violations and reducing them by approximately 10$\times$ across multiple correction rounds---demonstrating the detect-then-fix paradigm's effectiveness but also its inherent multi-pass cost.
\citet{upadhyay2023openie} inject entity-type knowledge as constraints into Open IE via both constrained inference and constraint-aware training, improving F1 by 29\% on CaRB, though their constrained inference operates over a discrete candidate set rather than during autoregressive generation.
\citet{regino2025kgcurator} propose a multi-stage LLM pipeline for validating RDF triple insertions against RDFS domain/range constraints, where each validation step requires a separate LLM call---effective but computationally expensive at scale.
RELATE~\cite{olasunkanmi2025relate} addresses the alignment gap between LLM-extracted biomedical relations and standardized ontology predicates through a three-stage pipeline: ontology preprocessing with predicate embeddings, similarity-based retrieval via SapBERT, and LLM-based reranking with negation handling, achieving 94\% accuracy@10 on ChemProt.
While RELATE demonstrates effective ontology grounding for relation extraction, its constraints are applied \emph{post-extraction} through retrieval and reranking rather than during generation, and it requires domain-specific embedding models trained on biomedical corpora.
OntoCoDec enforces ontology constraints \emph{during} autoregressive decoding and requires no additional trained components beyond the base LLM.
Concurrently, \citet{zhou2026ontologytools} compile OWL ontologies into executable tool interfaces within The World Avatar framework, requiring LLM agents to invoke ontology-aware tools that enforce semantic constraints during knowledge graph construction from scientific text.
This ``ontology-to-tools'' approach shares OntoCoDec's philosophy of compiling formal ontological knowledge into runtime enforcement mechanisms, but operates at the tool-call level (constraining which API functions the agent invokes) rather than at the token level (constraining which tokens the decoder produces), and requires an agentic multi-step workflow rather than single-pass autoregressive generation.
\citet{ekaw2024_ontology_beam} introduce ontology-constrained beam scoring for clinical summarization, applying soft biases (not hard masks) during beam search to steer outputs toward ontology-compliant terms---a middle ground between unconstrained generation and hard enforcement that reduces but cannot eliminate violations.
Post-hoc validation detects violations after generation, requiring rejection or correction cycles that waste compute---in our setting, 15.37\% of generated triples contain domain/range violations under unconstrained decoding, representing substantial wasted generation effort.
OntoCoDec \emph{prevents} violations during decoding, redirecting probability mass to valid alternatives rather than discarding invalid outputs, with only marginal overhead from logits masking compared to the cost of regenerating or correcting violated triples.
Soft-constraint approaches such as ontology-weighted beam scoring reduce violation frequency but cannot eliminate it, whereas OntoCoDec substantially reduces violations (DR$\downarrow$94\% on SciERC, $\downarrow$45\% on DocRED).

% ===========================================================================
% Paradigm 5: Constrained Decoding Quality Concerns
% ===========================================================================
\paragraph{Quality Impact of Constrained Decoding.}
A growing body of work raises concerns that constrained decoding degrades LLM generation quality, particularly for reasoning-intensive tasks where format enforcement interferes with chain-of-thought processes.
\citet{tam2024letmespeak} conduct a comprehensive evaluation showing that rigid format constraints (JSON, XML) harm performance on math and multi-hop QA benchmarks but \emph{benefit} classification-style tasks such as slot filling---a distinction directly relevant to IE, which is fundamentally an extraction (classification-like) task rather than a reasoning task.
CRANE~\cite{banerjee2025crane} provides theoretical analysis of why restricting outputs to narrow grammars suppresses chain-of-thought reasoning by eliminating intermediate reasoning tokens, and proposes an alternating strategy between unconstrained reasoning phases and constrained output phases to mitigate this effect.
\citet{schall2025hiddencost} conduct a systematic study across 11 models and multiple benchmarks, finding 10--30\% semantic correctness degradation on reasoning tasks under structural constraints, with larger models showing greater absolute degradation.
\citet{zhou2026snowballing} identify ``structure snowballing''---a failure mode where format compliance cognitive load traps models in repetitive structural patterns rather than improving reasoning during self-correction iterations.
These findings establish a legitimate concern for constrained decoding in reasoning-heavy applications.
However, information extraction occupies a fundamentally different regime: the model extracts entities and relations from input text rather than generating novel reasoning chains, and \citet{tam2024letmespeak}'s own results show that extraction-style tasks are robust to---or even benefit from---format constraints.
OntoCoDec addresses this concern empirically: domain/range violations decrease by 94\% on SciERC (15.37\%$\to$0.93\%) and 45\% on DocRED, with \emph{zero} F1 degradation on SciERC (R-F1 8.36\% vs.\ 8.23\% unconstrained, $+$0.13pp, not statistically significant).
Critically, OntoCoDec's constraints target only type tokens (entity types, relation labels), leaving free-text spans---entity surface forms and their boundaries---entirely unconstrained, which minimizes the distribution distortion that causes quality degradation in reasoning tasks.
A two-pass variant (S2), explored in ablation (Section~5), separates extraction and constraint enforcement into distinct passes, analogous to CRANE's alternating strategy; however, our primary single-pass approach already avoids reasoning interference by constraining only type tokens while leaving free-text spans unconstrained.

% ===========================================================================
% Our Approach
% ===========================================================================
\paragraph{Our Approach.}
OntoCoDec occupies a unique position in this landscape: it is the first system to \emph{automatically compile} IE ontology schemas---including domain/range axioms---into token-level semantic masks, extending grammar-constrained decoding from syntactic to semantic enforcement without manually authored rules.
Unlike vocabulary-constrained methods that restrict individual tokens to a fixed set, OntoCoDec enforces \emph{cross-field relational constraints} through a stateful entity registry that tracks extracted types during autoregressive generation, enabling dynamic constraint evaluation that depends on previously decoded content.
This approach is orthogonal to supervised IE methods and applicable to any autoregressive LM without model modification or additional training.
Unlike training-based IE systems, OntoCoDec is training-free and substantially reduces type violations at inference time (DR$\downarrow$94\% on SciERC, $\downarrow$45\% on DocRED); unlike post-hoc validation, it prevents violations rather than detecting them, redirecting probability mass to valid alternatives with zero quality cost on SciERC (R-F1 8.36\% vs.\ 8.23\% unconstrained).
The two constraint layers---grammar (structural) and semantic (relational)---compose via bitwise AND with an enabling dependency: the grammar layer ensures every generated type token belongs to the valid vocabulary, which enables the semantic layer to look up and enforce domain/range rules for that type.

\paragraph{Practical Significance of Zero-Shot F1.}
Our reported relation F1 of approximately 8\% on both SciERC and DocRED reflects the inherent difficulty of zero-shot closed IE, where the model receives no task-specific training examples.
For reference, supervised state-of-the-art systems on SciERC achieve approximately 49--53\% relation F1 with full training data~\citep{zhong2021frustratingly,ye2022packed}.
Constraint enforcement operates largely independently of the extraction model's intrinsic capability: it restricts the output space to ontologically valid triples regardless of the underlying model's accuracy.
When applied to fine-tuned models that reach competitive F1 levels, the same constraints remain necessary---Phase~0 analysis confirms that even well-prompted models exhibit non-trivial violation rates (15.37\% DR on SciERC, 18.46\% on DocRED).
% exp_ids: phase0_scierc_unconstrained, phase2_docred_unconstrained
In our evaluation, F1 serves as a \emph{control variable} verifying that constraint enforcement does not degrade extraction quality, not as an optimization target.
The contribution of this work is the constraint enforcement method itself; the zero-shot setting isolates its effect from confounds introduced by task-specific fine-tuning.

% exp_ids: posthoc_filtering_baseline, phase2_scierc_full_s1 (R-F1=8.36%),
%          phase2_docred_full_s1 (R-F1=8.23%, ET=0%)

\paragraph{Decoding-Time vs.\ Post-Hoc Enforcement.}
Post-hoc filtering---generating triples without constraints, then removing schema-violating predictions---yields higher precision and consequently higher F1 than OntoCoDec on both datasets (SciERC 8.63 vs.\ 8.36; DocRED 9.61 vs.\ 8.23).
% posthoc: SciERC F1=8.63, DocRED F1=9.61; OntoCoDec: SciERC R-F1=8.36, DocRED R-F1=8.23
However, this precision gain comes at substantial cost.
On DocRED, post-hoc filtering discards 48.1\% of all predicted triples, including 127 true positives (11.2\% of correct predictions), reducing recall from 9.46\% to 8.40\%.
% posthoc_docred: rejection=48.1%, tp_lost=127/1137, R: 9.46→8.40
Entity type violations remain unresolved (ET\,=\,2.47\% vs.\ OntoCoDec's 0\%), as filtering targets only domain/range and vocabulary violations.
% posthoc_docred: ET_residual=2.47%; phase2_docred_full_s1: ET=0%
OntoCoDec's decoding-time approach avoids this information loss by guiding generation toward compliant outputs rather than discarding non-compliant ones, preserving both recall and entity type validity.
The two strategies are complementary: post-hoc filtering can serve as an additional safety net for residual violations that decoding-time enforcement does not fully resolve.

% Section 5 — SciERC Results (Draft)
% Data source: Phase 2 SciERC registry experiments
% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_unconstrained, phase2_scierc_grammar_only,
%          phase2_scierc_semantic_only, phase2_scierc_full_s1, phase2_scierc_full_s2
% All numbers verified against registry 2026-05-14.

\subsection{Results on SciERC}
\label{sec:scierc-results}

Table~\ref{tab:scierc-ablation} presents the five-way ablation on SciERC,
evaluating each constraint layer independently and in combination.
All experiments use Qwen3-8B in a zero-shot setting on 551 test documents
with identical prompts and decoding parameters;
only the active constraint layers differ.

% Table: SciERC five-way ablation
\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3.6pt}
\begin{tabular}{@{}l rrrrr rr@{}}
\toprule
& \multicolumn{5}{c}{\textbf{Violation Rates (\%)}}
& \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{F1}} \\
\cmidrule(lr){2-6} \cmidrule(l){7-8}
\textbf{Mode}
  & DR\,$\downarrow$ & $\Delta$DR
  & RV\,$\downarrow$ & ET\,$\downarrow$ & CF
  & Rel.\,$\uparrow$ & Ent.\,$\uparrow$ \\
\midrule
Unconstrained
  & 15.37 & ---
  & 1.39  & 0.40
  & 0.08
  & 8.23  & 31.01 \\
Grammar
  & 14.84 & $\downarrow$3\%
  & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0}
  & 0.08
  & 8.23  & 30.98 \\
Semantic
  & 11.65 & $\downarrow$24\%
  & 1.51  & 0.40
  & 2.71
  & 8.15  & 31.01 \\
Full (S1)
  & \textbf{0.93} & $\downarrow$\textbf{94\%}
  & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0}
  & 9.90
  & \textbf{8.36} & 30.98 \\
Full (S2)
  & 0.97  & $\downarrow$94\%
  & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0}
  & 8.03
  & 8.03  & \textbf{31.90} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Five-way ablation on SciERC (551 documents, Qwen3-8B, zero-shot).
DR: domain/range violation rate;
RV: relation vocabulary violation rate;
ET: entity type violation rate;
CF: cross-field consistency violation rate.
$\Delta$DR: relative DR reduction vs.\ the unconstrained baseline.
$\downarrow$\,/\,$\uparrow$: lower\,/\,higher is better.
Best per column in \textbf{bold} (CF excluded---see text).
F1 scores are multiplied by 100.
Statistical significance assessed via bootstrap resampling (10{,}000 iterations).}
\label{tab:scierc-ablation}
\end{table}

% (a) Core result
\paragraph{Core result: DR elimination at zero F1 cost.}
The full two-layer constraint configuration (S1) reduces domain/range
violations from 15.37\% to 0.93\%, a 94\% relative reduction,
% phase2_scierc_unconstrained: DR=0.1537; phase2_scierc_full_s1: DR=0.0093
while relation F1 moves from 8.23 to 8.36 ($+$0.13\,pp; bootstrap 95\% CI [$-$0.24, $+$0.58]\,pp, $p = 0.58$, 10{,}000 iterations).
% phase2_scierc_unconstrained: R-F1=0.0823; phase2_scierc_full_s1: R-F1=0.0836
% bootstrap: delta=+0.13pp, CI=[-0.24,+0.58], p=0.5824
The difference is not statistically significant ($p = 0.58$), confirming
that constraint enforcement is F1-neutral on this dataset.
At the per-relation level, violations drop from 42.42\% to 2.82\% on
\textsc{Compare}, from 33.54\% to 1.21\% on \textsc{Feature-of}, and
reach 0\% on four of seven relation types
(\textsc{Conjunction}, \textsc{Hyponym-of}, \textsc{Part-of},
\textsc{Used-for}).
% phase2_scierc_full_s1 per_relation_dr: Compare=0.0282,
%   Feature-of=0.0121, Hyponym-of=0, Part-of=0, Used-for=0, Conjunction=0
However, full constraint enforcement elevates cross-field consistency
violations from 0.08\% to 9.90\%;
% phase2_scierc_unconstrained: CF=0.0008; phase2_scierc_full_s1: CF=0.099
we analyze this trade-off in Section~\ref{sec:discussion}.

% (b) Grammar layer
\paragraph{Grammar layer: cost-free structural guarantees.}
Grammar-only constraints completely eliminate both relation vocabulary
violations (1.39\%\,$\to$\,0\%) and entity type violations
(0.40\%\,$\to$\,0\%), with no measurable impact on F1
(R-F1 8.23, E-F1 30.98).
% phase2_scierc_grammar_only: RV=0, ET=0, R-F1=0.0823, E-F1=0.3098
Domain/range violations remain effectively unchanged
(15.37\%\,$\to$\,14.84\%, $-$0.53\,pp), confirming that grammar
constraints enforce output structure---valid JSON, correct relation
vocabulary, valid entity types---but do not address cross-field
semantic constraints.
% phase2_scierc_grammar_only: DR=0.1484
The grammar layer thus provides two categories of violation elimination
at zero cost, establishing the structural preconditions on which the
semantic layer depends.

% (c) Enabling dependency
\paragraph{Enabling dependency: grammar enables semantic enforcement.}
Applying semantic constraints alone reduces DR by only 24\%
(15.37\%\,$\to$\,11.65\%) and, critically, cannot eliminate
relation vocabulary violations (RV\,=\,1.51\%) or entity type
violations (ET\,=\,0.40\%).
% phase2_scierc_semantic_only: DR=0.1165, RV=0.0151, ET=0.004
When the grammar layer is added (Full S1), DR drops a further 92\%
relative to the semantic-only configuration
(11.65\%\,$\to$\,0.93\%).
% phase2_scierc_full_s1: DR=0.0093; delta=(11.65-0.93)/11.65=0.920
This demonstrates an \emph{enabling dependency} rather than mere
additivity: without grammar-enforced vocabulary constraints, the
semantic layer encounters out-of-vocabulary relation types for which
no domain/range rules exist, rendering its type checking ineffective.
The two layers are therefore complementary with a prerequisite
structure---grammar must be active for semantic constraints to reach
their full enforcement capacity.

% (d) S1 vs S2
\paragraph{S1 vs.\ S2: single-pass suffices.}
The two-pass strategy (S2) achieves comparable DR
(0.97\% vs.\ 0.93\%) but lower relation F1
(8.03 vs.\ 8.36, $-$0.33\,pp) and generates fewer relation triples
(1{,}644 vs.\ 1{,}729).
% phase2_scierc_full_s2: DR=0.0097, R-F1=0.0803, triples=1644
% phase2_scierc_full_s1: DR=0.0093, R-F1=0.0836, triples=1729
S2 shows a modestly lower CF rate (8.03\% vs.\ 9.90\%), but both
configurations exhibit substantially elevated CF relative to the
unconstrained baseline (0.08\%), indicating that two-pass decoding
does not resolve the cross-field consistency trade-off
(Section~\ref{sec:discussion}).
% phase2_scierc_full_s2: CF=0.0803; phase2_scierc_full_s1: CF=0.099
The two-pass separation offers no clear advantage over single-pass
enforcement; we adopt S1 as the primary configuration for its
simplicity and marginally stronger extraction performance.
TEXEOF

\label{tab:docred-ablation}
\end{table}

% exp_ids: phase2_docred_unconstrained, phase2_docred_full_s1
\paragraph{Core result.}
Full S1 reduces DR from 18.46\% to 10.21\% ($\downarrow$45\%), eliminates ET (2.48\%\,$\to$\,0\%), and near-eliminates RV (29.66\%\,$\to$\,0.03\%).
Relation F1 improves from 7.74 to 8.23 ($+$0.50\,pp; bootstrap 95\% CI [$+$0.23, $+$0.81], $p < 0.001$), attributable to grammar-layer elimination of 5{,}189 OOV relation predictions counted as false positives.
CF increases modestly (0.10\%\,$\to$\,2.57\%), lower than SciERC's 9.90\%.

% exp_ids: phase2_docred_grammar_only
\paragraph{Grammar layer surfaces latent violations.}
Grammar-only constraints eliminate RV and ET but \emph{increase} DR from 18.46\% to 26.17\% ($+$42\%).
This counter-intuitive result has a structural explanation: the unconstrained baseline's 29.66\% OOV relation triples cannot be evaluated for DR (no schema entry exists); grammar enforcement assigns these triples valid relation names whose domain/range rules the associated entity types frequently violate.
The grammar layer thus \emph{reveals} latent type incompatibilities, directly motivating the semantic layer.

% exp_ids: phase2_docred_semantic_only, phase2_docred_full_s1
\paragraph{Enabling dependency.}
Semantic-only constraints reduce DR by only 25\% (18.46\%\,$\to$\,13.84\%) while failing to eliminate RV (29.87\%) or ET (4.22\%).
Full S1 achieves a further 26\% relative reduction over semantic-only (13.84\%\,$\to$\,10.21\%), replicating the enabling dependency from SciERC: without grammar-enforced vocabulary, the semantic layer encounters OOV relation types for which no domain/range rules exist.

% exp_ids: phase2_docred_full_s1, llama_docred_full_s1
\paragraph{Constraint tightness governs enforcement ceiling.}
The residual DR on DocRED (10.21\%) exceeds SciERC (0.93\%) due to per-relation \emph{constraint tightness}: DocRED relations average 5.68 valid type pairs ($\bar{\tau}{=}0.842$) vs.\ 24 on SciERC ($\bar{\tau}{=}0.333$).

This dual-factor mechanism---tightness $\times$ baseline RV---explains cross-dataset and cross-model DR reduction differences.

\section{Extended Related Work}
\label{app:related_work}

\paragraph{Grammar-Constrained Decoding.}
Recent work has established efficient algorithms for restricting LLM outputs to conform to context-free grammars, making grammar-constrained decoding the de facto standard for obtaining structured output from language models.
XGrammar~\cite{dong2025xgrammar} partitions the vocabulary into context-independent and context-dependent tokens and maintains persistent pushdown automata across decoding steps, achieving up to 100$\times$ speedup over prior CFG-constrained decoding methods.
Outlines~\cite{willard2023outlines} reformulates constrained generation as finite-state machine transitions with offline vocabulary indexing, enabling efficient enforcement of regular-expression and JSON-schema constraints without runtime overhead per token.
LMQL~\cite{beurer-kellner2023lmql} introduces a declarative query language that compiles type, length, and regex constraints into token-level masks, providing a programmable interface for specifying multi-variable output structures.
These systems ensure that every generated token belongs to a grammar-valid continuation, but they do not address the \emph{distribution distortion} introduced by naive token masking.
A parallel line of work tackles this problem directly: DOMINO~\cite{beurer-kellner2024domino} minimizes distributional divergence during CFG enforcement by formulating mask selection as an optimization problem, and ASAp~\cite{park2024grammar} provides a provably unbiased sampling algorithm that preserves the original LM distribution under grammar constraints.
Together, these advances have made grammar-constrained decoding both fast and statistically principled, establishing a robust foundation for structured generation.
However, all of these methods operate exclusively at the syntactic level---they ensure format validity (e.g., well-formed JSON, valid enum values) but cannot enforce cross-field semantic constraints such as ontology domain/range rules that depend on previously generated content.
This syntactic-only limitation motivates OntoCoDec's semantic extension: our grammar layer builds on XGrammar for structural (JSON schema and enum) constraints, while a second semantic layer enforces relational type constraints that are inherently beyond the expressive power of context-free grammars.

\paragraph{Semantic Constrained Decoding for Code.}
In programming-language generation, constrained decoding has been extended beyond syntax to enforce semantic properties such as type correctness, demonstrating that richer-than-CFG constraints can be compiled into token-level filtering.
In the text-to-SQL domain, PICARD~\cite{scholak2021picard} maintains an incremental SQL parsing state that rejects tokens violating syntax or referencing non-existent database columns at each decoding step, achieving state-of-the-art results on Spider and CoSQL without modifying model weights.
While mechanistically similar to OntoCoDec's token-level filtering, PICARD operates over a \emph{fixed, fully enumerated} schema---database table and column names known before decoding begins.
In contrast, OntoCoDec's entity registry is populated \emph{during} generation as entity spans are extracted from free text, requiring constraint sets that evolve with the decoding prefix---a fundamental distinction between querying a known schema and extracting from unstructured text.
Synchromesh~\cite{synchromesh_iclr2022} pioneers Constrained Semantic Decoding (CSD), which enforces syntax, type, and scope constraints simultaneously during code generation from pre-trained LMs without fine-tuning, establishing that semantic constraints can be expressed as dynamic token masks conditioned on the generation prefix.
MGD~\cite{mgd_neurips2023} uses static-analysis monitors to perform incremental type checking at decode time, enabling SantaCoder-1.1B to outperform text-davinci-003 on repository-level code completion by ensuring that every generated identifier is type-correct with respect to the surrounding code context.
Most recently, \citet{pldi2025_type_constrained_codegen} compile full type systems---including generic types and subtyping---into prefix automata for token-level logits masking, reducing compilation errors by over 50\%.
This last system is the closest mechanistic analog to OntoCoDec, applying the same ``type system $\to$ automaton $\to$ logits mask'' pipeline, though in a fundamentally different domain.
The key technical difference lies in the constraint structure: programming-language type systems feature deep subtyping hierarchies and parametric polymorphism, whereas IE ontology axioms specify flat domain/range sets---a relation $R$ accepts head entities from set $\mathcal{D}(R)$ and tail entities from set $\mathcal{R}(R)$, with no subtype chains.
Conversely, IE introduces a challenge absent in code generation: the constraint target (entity type) must be inferred from free-text spans rather than read from declared type annotations, requiring a stateful entity registry that tracks extracted types during autoregressive generation.
These methods collectively demonstrate that semantic (type) constraints at decode time are both feasible and highly effective, but exclusively in the code domain where type systems are formally specified.
OntoCoDec is the first to \emph{automatically compile} IE ontology axioms---including domain/range constraints---into token-level decoding masks for information extraction, migrating the type-constrained decoding paradigm from code generation to IE.

\paragraph{Vocabulary and Type-Constrained Generation.}
The idea of enforcing entity-type compatibility constraints for information extraction dates back to pre-neural methods.
\citet{roth_yih_2004} formulate joint entity and relation identification as an integer linear program (ILP) that enforces type constraints---e.g., \textsc{Emp-Org} only between \textsc{Per} and \textsc{Org} entities---establishing the foundational principle that relational type compatibility should be a hard constraint, not a soft preference learned from data.
In the autoregressive era, GENRE~\cite{decao2021genre} pioneers trie-based constrained beam search for autoregressive entity retrieval, restricting each decoding step to tokens consistent with valid entity names from a predefined catalog.
GenIE~\cite{josifoski2022genie} extends this approach to end-to-end information extraction with state-based constraints that enforce valid triple structures, achieving strong performance on closed-world knowledge base population, though it requires task-specific fine-tuning on the target schema.
AdaKGC~\cite{adakgc_emnlp2023} introduces schema-constrained dynamic decoding with trie-based prefix trees that adapt to the target schema, enforcing that generated entity and relation names belong to a predefined inventory---a vocabulary-level constraint that ensures name validity but does not verify type compatibility between a relation and its arguments.
GCD~\cite{geng2023gcd} provides a unified grammar-constrained decoding framework for structured NLP tasks including IE, introducing input-dependent grammars that adapt constraints based on the source text---the closest precursor to OntoCoDec in applying logits masking to IE, though limited to syntactic constraints.
NeuroLogic Decoding~\cite{lu2021neurologic} expresses lexical inclusion and exclusion constraints as predicate logic formulas enforced during beam search, offering a general mechanism for token-level control that can encode vocabulary membership but not relational type rules.
These approaches constrain \emph{which tokens} can appear (vocabulary membership) but not \emph{which type combinations} are valid for a given relation.
OntoCoDec's semantic layer enforces relational constraints---e.g., that the head entity of relation $R$ must belong to type set $\mathcal{D}(R)$---which cannot be expressed as static vocabulary restrictions because the valid set depends on the relation type generated earlier in the same sequence.
While Roth \& Yih's ILP formulation shares the same type-compatibility motivation, it operates as a post-hoc reranker over discrete candidates; OntoCoDec integrates enforcement directly into autoregressive decoding, preventing violations rather than filtering them.

\paragraph{Structural Constraints via Training and Prompting.}
An orthogonal approach encodes IE output structure through model training or prompt design rather than decoding-time enforcement, relying on learned representations to produce schema-compliant outputs.
UIE~\cite{lu2022uie} defines a Structured Extraction Language and trains a unified text-to-structure model across 13 IE datasets, relying on large-scale pre-training to internalize output format constraints.
GoLLIE~\cite{sainz2024gollie} expresses annotation guidelines as Python dataclass definitions and fine-tunes Code-LLaMA to generate typed code, achieving strong zero-shot transfer to unseen IE schemas by leveraging the implicit type structure of programming languages.
KnowCoder~\cite{knowcoder_acl2024} takes this further by encoding 29K entity types from Wikidata as a Python class hierarchy, training a Code-LLM to generate structured extraction code that implicitly respects type inheritance---the most comprehensive schema-as-code approach to date.
CodeIE~\cite{li2023codeie} similarly reformulates IE as code generation, leveraging the structural regularity of programming languages to reduce output format errors.
ADELIE~\cite{qi2024adelie} uses SFT and DPO to align LLMs on IE tasks, achieving state-of-the-art results among open-source models while preserving general capabilities, though compliance with ontological constraints remains a learned soft preference rather than a guarantee.
In the supervised setting, joint entity-relation architectures such as SpERT~\cite{eberts2020spert} and PFN~\cite{yan2021pfn} enforce type consistency implicitly through shared representations: SpERT classifies entity spans and relation pairs in a single BERT pass with span-level negative sampling, while PFN decomposes feature encoding into entity-specific, relation-specific, and shared partitions via gating mechanisms.
These models achieve strong performance but are limited to fixed, predefined schemas and cannot generalize to unseen ontologies without retraining---precisely the zero-shot, ontology-portable scenario that OntoCoDec targets.
EnriCo~\cite{zaratiana2024enrico} applies Answer Set Programming (ASP) constraints during decoding of joint entity-relation extraction models, enforcing structural type compatibility at generation time---a decoding-time approach, though with model-specific, manually authored constraints rather than ontology-driven compilation.
Training-based methods provide \emph{soft} structural guidance---the model learns to prefer valid outputs but cannot guarantee compliance at inference time, as demonstrated by non-trivial violation rates even in fine-tuned systems.
Importantly, training-based and decoding-time approaches are complementary rather than competing: a system like GoLLIE could be combined with OntoCoDec's constraint layers, using fine-tuning to maximize the probability of valid outputs while decoding-time enforcement eliminates residual violations.
OntoCoDec provides \emph{hard} decoding-time enforcement that is training-free, automatically compiled from ontology schemas, and composable with any of these training-based approaches.

\paragraph{Post-hoc Ontology Validation.}
Rather than constraining generation, several methods validate LLM outputs against ontological rules after generation, applying a detect-then-fix paradigm.
ODKE+~\cite{khorshidi2025odke} dynamically generates ontology snippets containing domain/range constraints as prompt context, achieving 98.8\% precision across 195 predicates at web scale---but constraint adherence relies on prompt-level guidance, not enforcement, leaving residual violations unaddressed.
SPIRES/OntoGPT~\cite{spires_2024} provides an ontology-based extraction framework that grounds LLM outputs against OBO ontologies post-generation, validating extracted entities and relations through ontology lookup and correcting mismatches in a second pass---representing the prompt-then-validate paradigm in the biomedical domain.
OntoLogX~\cite{ontologx_2025} applies SHACL validation to LLM-generated knowledge graphs, iteratively re-prompting the LLM to correct constraint violations and reducing them by approximately 10$\times$ across multiple correction rounds---demonstrating the detect-then-fix paradigm's effectiveness but also its inherent multi-pass cost.
\citet{upadhyay2023openie} inject entity-type knowledge as constraints into Open IE via both constrained inference and constraint-aware training, improving F1 by 29\% on CaRB, though their constrained inference operates over a discrete candidate set rather than during autoregressive generation.
\citet{regino2025kgcurator} propose a multi-stage LLM pipeline for validating RDF triple insertions against RDFS domain/range constraints, where each validation step requires a separate LLM call---effective but computationally expensive at scale.
RELATE~\cite{olasunkanmi2025relate} addresses the alignment gap between LLM-extracted biomedical relations and standardized ontology predicates through a three-stage pipeline: ontology preprocessing with predicate embeddings, similarity-based retrieval via SapBERT, and LLM-based reranking with negation handling, achieving 94\% accuracy@10 on ChemProt.
While RELATE demonstrates effective ontology grounding for relation extraction, its constraints are applied \emph{post-extraction} through retrieval and reranking rather than during generation, and it requires domain-specific embedding models trained on biomedical corpora.
OntoCoDec enforces ontology constraints \emph{during} autoregressive decoding and requires no additional trained components beyond the base LLM.
Concurrently, \citet{zhou2026ontologytools} compile OWL ontologies into executable tool interfaces within The World Avatar framework, requiring LLM agents to invoke ontology-aware tools that enforce semantic constraints during knowledge graph construction from scientific text.
This ``ontology-to-tools'' approach shares OntoCoDec's philosophy of compiling formal ontological knowledge into runtime enforcement mechanisms, but operates at the tool-call level (constraining which API functions the agent invokes) rather than at the token level (constraining which tokens the decoder produces), and requires an agentic multi-step workflow rather than single-pass autoregressive generation.
\citet{ekaw2024_ontology_beam} introduce ontology-constrained beam scoring for clinical summarization, applying soft biases (not hard masks) during beam search to steer outputs toward ontology-compliant terms---a middle ground between unconstrained generation and hard enforcement that reduces but cannot eliminate violations.
Post-hoc validation detects violations after generation, requiring rejection or correction cycles that waste compute---in our setting, 15.37\% of generated triples contain domain/range violations under unconstrained decoding, representing substantial wasted generation effort.
OntoCoDec \emph{prevents} violations during decoding, redirecting probability mass to valid alternatives rather than discarding invalid outputs, with only marginal overhead from logits masking compared to the cost of regenerating or correcting violated triples.
Soft-constraint approaches such as ontology-weighted beam scoring reduce violation frequency but cannot eliminate it, whereas OntoCoDec substantially reduces violations (DR$\downarrow$94\% on SciERC, $\downarrow$45\% on DocRED).

\paragraph{Quality Impact of Constrained Decoding.}
A growing body of work raises concerns that constrained decoding degrades LLM generation quality, particularly for reasoning-intensive tasks where format enforcement interferes with chain-of-thought processes.
\citet{tam2024letmespeak} conduct a comprehensive evaluation showing that rigid format constraints (JSON, XML) harm performance on math and multi-hop QA benchmarks but \emph{benefit} classification-style tasks such as slot filling---a distinction directly relevant to IE, which is fundamentally an extraction (classification-like) task rather than a reasoning task.
CRANE~\cite{banerjee2025crane} provides theoretical analysis of why restricting outputs to narrow grammars suppresses chain-of-thought reasoning by eliminating intermediate reasoning tokens, and proposes an alternating strategy between unconstrained reasoning phases and constrained output phases to mitigate this effect.
\citet{schall2025hiddencost} conduct a systematic study across 11 models and multiple benchmarks, finding 10--30\% semantic correctness degradation on reasoning tasks under structural constraints, with larger models showing greater absolute degradation.
\citet{zhou2026snowballing} identify ``structure snowballing''---a failure mode where format compliance cognitive load traps models in repetitive structural patterns rather than improving reasoning during self-correction iterations.
These findings establish a legitimate concern for constrained decoding in reasoning-heavy applications.
However, information extraction occupies a fundamentally different regime: the model extracts entities and relations from input text rather than generating novel reasoning chains, and \citet{tam2024letmespeak}'s own results show that extraction-style tasks are robust to---or even benefit from---format constraints.
OntoCoDec addresses this concern empirically: domain/range violations decrease by 94\% on SciERC (15.37\%$\to$0.93\%) and 45\% on DocRED, with \emph{zero} F1 degradation on SciERC (R-F1 8.36\% vs.\ 8.23\% unconstrained, $+$0.13pp, not statistically significant).
Critically, OntoCoDec's constraints target only type tokens (entity types, relation labels), leaving free-text spans---entity surface forms and their boundaries---entirely unconstrained, which minimizes the distribution distortion that causes quality degradation in reasoning tasks.
A two-pass variant (S2), explored in ablation (Section~5), separates extraction and constraint enforcement into distinct passes, analogous to CRANE's alternating strategy; however, our primary single-pass approach already avoids reasoning interference by constraining only type tokens while leaving free-text spans unconstrained.

\paragraph{Our Approach.}
OntoCoDec occupies a unique position in this landscape: it is the first system to \emph{automatically compile} IE ontology schemas---including domain/range axioms---into token-level semantic masks, extending grammar-constrained decoding from syntactic to semantic enforcement without manually authored rules.
Unlike vocabulary-constrained methods that restrict individual tokens to a fixed set, OntoCoDec enforces \emph{cross-field relational constraints} through a stateful entity registry that tracks extracted types during autoregressive generation, enabling dynamic constraint evaluation that depends on previously decoded content.
This approach is orthogonal to supervised IE methods and applicable to any autoregressive LM without model modification or additional training.
Unlike training-based IE systems, OntoCoDec is training-free and substantially reduces type violations at inference time (DR$\downarrow$94\% on SciERC, $\downarrow$45\% on DocRED); unlike post-hoc validation, it prevents violations rather than detecting them, redirecting probability mass to valid alternatives with zero quality cost on SciERC (R-F1 8.36\% vs.\ 8.23\% unconstrained).
The two constraint layers---grammar (structural) and semantic (relational)---compose via bitwise AND with an enabling dependency: the grammar layer ensures every generated type token belongs to the valid vocabulary, which enables the semantic layer to look up and enforce domain/range rules for that type.

OntoCoDec's decoding-time approach avoids this information loss by guiding generation toward compliant outputs rather than discarding non-compliant ones, preserving both recall and entity type validity.
